title: Moon to Gobble Up the Sun Next Week! Here's How to Watch
summary: Have you ever seen the sky go dark in the middle of the day? That's what happens during a total solar eclipse, and one is coming on Wednesday! The moon will slide right in front of the sun, blocking its light for a few magical minutes. People in Iceland, Greenland, northern Russia, Spain, and a bit of Portugal will get the full show — the sky will turn twilight-dark, and you might even see stars. In the U.S., from Alaska all the way to North Carolina, you'll see a partial eclipse, where the sun looks like a glowing crescent cookie. In Washington, D.C., the fun starts around 1:17 p.m. ET, but only about 4% of the sun will be covered — just a tiny nibble. In Reykjavík, Iceland, the total eclipse begins at 5:48 p.m. local time, and in León, Spain, it starts at 8:28 p.m. and lasts two whole minutes. This is super special for Spain — it's the first total solar eclipse visible from its mainland since 1905, more than 120 years ago! If you want to watch, you MUST wear special eclipse glasses. Regular sunglasses won't protect your eyes, and looking at the sun — even for a second — can burn your eyes and cause permanent damage. Scientists are excited too. NASA will launch balloons and fly a high-altitude jet to study how the sudden darkness changes Earth's atmosphere. They want to learn more about the sun's corona, its outer atmosphere, which is usually hidden by the sun's glare. So grab your glasses, find a clear spot, and look up (safely!). If you miss this one, a partial eclipse visits the U.S. again on August 2, 2027, but the next total eclipse across the whole country won't happen until August 23, 2044 — that's a long wait!
why_it_matters: Watching a solar eclipse is a rare chance to see a spectacular natural wonder and learn about space — maybe one day you'll become a scientist who studies the stars!

questions.question: What causes the sky to go dark during a total solar eclipse?
options: The moon covers the sun completely.
The Earth turns away from the sun.
The sun stops shining for a few minutes.
questions.correct_answer: The moon covers the sun completely.

background_read: A total solar eclipse happens somewhere on Earth roughly every 18 months, but any single spot only sees one every few hundred years.
Thousands of years ago, many people were afraid of eclipses and thought a dragon or giant animal was eating the sun.
Article_Structure: WHO: People in the path of the eclipse, especially in Iceland, Greenland, Spain, Portugal, and parts of Russia; also skywatchers in the U.S.
WHAT: A total solar eclipse where the moon slips in front of the sun, turning day briefly into twilight.
WHERE: Total eclipse visible from a narrow path across Iceland, Greenland, northern Russia, Spain, and Portugal; a partial eclipse seen in the U.S.
WHY: Because the moon orbits Earth and sometimes it lines up exactly between Earth and the sun, casting a shadow.

perspectives.description: They are super excited to see the sun turn into a thin crescent and watch daylight become twilight — it feels magical!
They get a rare opportunity to study the sun's secret outer atmosphere with special planes and balloons, which helps us understand space better.
They worry that people might look without proper glasses and hurt their eyes permanently, so they remind everyone to be very careful.
